newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian government says safely on track for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Belgian government says safely on track for EMU.

text.p: The Belgian government said on Tuesday a 10.2 billion Belgian franc budget austerity package, details of which were made public on Monday, will keep it safely on track to take part in a single European currency.
Belgian Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy said the measures will ensure Belgium's deficit falls to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from 3.4 percent in 1996.

"The strict respect of our budget target has a triple safety margin," Van Rompuy told a news conference before Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene presented details of the package to parliament. Dehaene was due to begin his address at 1500 GMT.

Van Rompuy said the budget had a built in 20 billion Belgian franc safety margin which meant the 2.9 percent target could be hit even if short-term interest rates rose by 300 basis points above their current level of 3.60 percent.
Besides the interest rate margin, Van Rompuy said the budget was cautious because it assumed GDP growth of 2.1 percent in 1997, while most recent forecasts focus on 2.2 percent.
In addition, the 1997 budget set the deficit target at 2.9 percent, less than the maximum three percent limit foreseen in the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union (EMU).
A text of Van Rompuy's statement was headlined "Heading straight for the euro."
The 1997 budget, drawn up in October 1996, originally consisted of an 80 billion Belgian franc austerity package.
The 10.2 billion francs in extra measures, decided at the weekend during the government's annual budget review, was already the second correction to that original package.
In December last year the government pushed through 10 billion francs of savings in the health sector to compensate a spending overshoot.

Van Rompuy said the budget review had not targeted consumer spending. Instead, it mainly hits Belgium's corporate world and includes a further round of belt tightening in several federal government ministries.
A tax on the turnover of pharmaceutical companies will be increased to four percent from one percent, raising 1.8 billion francs in 1997.

Belgian utility company Electrabel NV, which has a virtual monopoly on electricity production in Belgium, will see the tax on its profits rise to 14 percent from 12 percent, raising 1.5 billion francs in 1997.
Electrabel said earlier this month that 1996 group net profit rose to 30.4 billion francs, from 28.8 billion in 1995.

Companies will also be hit by the obligation for non-managing partners in private companies to start paying withholding taxes on their income, which will no longer be seen as a profit, but as a salary. That measure will raise 1.2 billion francs this year.
A crackdown on evasion of value added taxes is expected to bring in an extra two billion francs, while spending cuts will save a total of three billion francs.

Defence will contribute 600 million francs, while the Development Cooperation Ministry will see its budget cut by 200 million. An unused 400 million franc budget for third world aid will also be taken back.
